title: I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:6–8)
hook: Paul near the end: I have fought a good fight, kept the faith
tomorrow: does God still speak today, or has he said it all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lois and Eunice: a grandmother, a mother, and a faith that dwelt in them first, then in Timothy. Yesterday's line: not a spirit of fear.
screen: `NOT A SPIRIT OF FEAR.` → `THE END OF THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Final messages are supposed to sound final. In the movie version there's a speech, a hand squeezed, a long look out a window. Near the end of Second Timothy, the writer is a prisoner who says his time is close, and he does write the big lines. Then, a few verses later, this: "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments." A coat. Something to read. Why is that in here?
screen: `FINAL WORDS SHOULD SOUND FINAL.` → `THE BIG LINES.` → `THEN: BRING MY COAT?`

segments.voice: First, the big lines. "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand." Then three short ones: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Three verbs, all done. The King James says course; the title says race. A runner's picture: the track laid out, run to the end. He doesn't say he won, or was fastest. He says he finished, and kept what was handed to him, the way someone keeps a promise. Then: "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness," and right away, "not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing." The finish line isn't a podium for one. Now the puzzle. Why the coat? Because finishing a course isn't the same as being finished with living. The man who has kept the faith is still cold, still wants to read, still misses his friends. Come soon, he writes; only Luke is with me. Faith kept to the end still asks for a coat, and the letter isn't embarrassed about it. One more line to tell a friend tonight. At his first hearing, he says, everyone deserted him, and then: "I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge." Finishing well, here, includes letting the ones who ran off the hook.
screen: `READY TO BE OFFERED.` · `FOUGHT, FINISHED, KEPT.` · `NOT TO ME ONLY.` · `STILL COLD, STILL READING.` · then, large: `I HAVE KEPT THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you've left half done that you can finish right where you are: a drawer, a reply, a loose button, a cup to rinse. Do the last step slowly and fully, so that when the sit begins, that one thing is finished. Then notice what it's like to have one thing done and put away.
I have finished the race. Paul's words near the end of Second Timothy: the course run to the end, the faith kept, and still a coat to ask for.
screen: `I HAVE FINISHED THE RACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to keep: I have kept the faith, finished and kept, and then, bring the coat. Rest well.

howItsDone: Some Christians read 2 Timothy 4:6–8 at funerals or near the end of a long service, as words for a life finished faithfully.

match.prompt: three verbs and a coat — tap the pairs.

myth: 'I have finished my course' means Paul won the race
he says fought, finished, kept the faith: no word about winning.
in the same chapter, Paul asks for his coat and his books
"the cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus… and the books, but especially the parchments."
Paul says the crown is for him alone
"not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing."

fork.setup: your coach retires and says at the banquet, 'i didn't win the most, but i finished.' someone whispers that's a sad thing to say. how does 2 Timothy 4 hear it?
options: as Paul's own kind of words: not won, but finished, and faith kept.
as giving up, since finishing only counts if you won.
as false modesty that Paul would have corrected.
fork.reveal: Paul doesn't claim to have won or been fastest. he says fought, finished, kept, and the crown is for all who love his appearing.

original.note: Greek: course, race; the King James renders it course in 2 Timothy 4:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: i have finished the race is a victory lap.
what it means: Paul names three finished things, a fight, a course, a kept faith, and says the crown waits for all who love his appearing.
what a scholar hears: the King James 'course' is a runner's track; and a few verses on, the same man asks for his cloak and his parchments.
guess: a course run to the end, the faith kept
first place won after a long contest
giving up because the end is too close

chat.says: pop's last sunday as deacon. he told the church 'i've finished my course.' sounds like goodbye-goodbye. is it?
options: Not always. Paul said it, then asked for his coat and books. A course done, life still going.
Yes. Paul only said it once there was nothing left to want or do.
No, it's a victory lap. Paul meant he'd won the race and beaten everyone else.
chat.meaning: Paul says I have finished my course, I have kept the faith, and a few verses later asks Timothy to bring his cloak and books.

Troas.meaning: a port town where Paul left his cloak

Carpus.meaning: the friend keeping Paul's cloak in Troas

cloke.meaning: the King James spelling of cloak, a heavy coat

parchments.meaning: writing material made from animal skin

notes: Puzzle shape: the strange detail is the request for the cloak and parchments (4:13) right after the 'finished' lines; solved as 'finishing a course isn't being finished with living'. That reading is the writer's; confirm.
The index word says 'race'; the King James 4:7 says 'course' (Greek dromos). The script says so plainly; confirm the Greek.
The draft's 'some readers hear an offering poured out' and 'a boat slipping its rope' were cut from the voice under the claims rule.
The letter names Paul as its writer; some scholars question whether Paul wrote the letters to Timothy. The script follows the text's own voice.
Gloss 'parchments' as writing material made from animal skin: general meaning of the English word; confirm.
